headline: Marcos Signs Law Expanding Tertiary Education Aid for Poorer Students
seoTitle: RA 12325 Expands Tertiary Education Aid in the Philippines | FMB News
seoDescription: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signed Republic Act No. 12325 on September 4, 2026, strengthening priority and financial support for poor and disadvantaged college and TVET students.
deck: Republic Act No. 12325 strengthens the country’s free tertiary education framework by giving poor and disadvantaged learners greater priority in government assistance and expanding support pathways for eligible college and technical-vocational students.
author: FMB News Desk

sections.heading: What happened
paragraphs: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signed Republic Act No. 12325 at Malacañang on Friday, September 4, amending the Universal Access to Quality Tertiary Education Act of 2017.

The new law strengthens the prioritization of government tertiary-education assistance for poor and disadvantaged students. Qualified beneficiaries of the Pantawid Pamilyang Pilipino Program are among those given priority under the expanded framework, while assistance may also support eligible learners in qualified private higher-education and technical-vocational institutions when they are not covered by existing grants.

sections.heading: Context
paragraphs: Republic Act No. 10931 established free tuition and other school-fee benefits in state universities and colleges, local universities and colleges, and state-run technical-vocational institutions, alongside student-aid programs such as the Tertiary Education Subsidy.

RA 12325 builds on that system by directing more support toward learners with greater financial need and by strengthening mechanisms for student financial assistance. The Commission on Higher Education said it would implement the expanded support for disadvantaged learners under the amended law.

sections.heading: Why this matters to Filipinos
paragraphs: For low-income families, the cost of tertiary education goes beyond tuition. Books, transport, housing, connectivity, equipment and other study-related expenses can still prevent students from completing a degree or technical-vocational program even when tuition is free.

The new law matters because it changes how limited assistance is prioritized and broadens the routes through which qualified students can receive support. Its impact will depend on implementing rules, available appropriations and how effectively agencies identify and serve eligible learners.

sections.heading: What to watch next
paragraphs: Watch for the implementing rules, program guidelines and budget allocations that will determine how RA 12325 is applied across higher-education and technical-vocational institutions.

Students and families should also watch for official guidance from CHED, UniFAST and relevant technical-vocational agencies on eligibility, application procedures and the specific assistance available under the strengthened framework.

audit.socialCaption: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has signed RA 12325, strengthening priority and financial support for poor and disadvantaged college and technical-vocational students. The next key step is implementation: eligibility rules, program guidance and funding will determine how the expanded assistance reaches students.
verificationNotes: The signing of RA 12325 on September 4, 2026 was confirmed by the Presidential Communications Office through PIA and by the Philippine News Agency.
The House of Representatives identified the enacted measure as Republic Act No. 12325 and described its strengthened priority for students most in need.
GMA News independently corroborated the signing and the expanded assistance for disadvantaged college students.
The article does not claim that all students will automatically receive a subsidy; eligibility and implementation remain subject to program rules and available government support.
No matching RA 12325 story was found in the September 4 FMB News repository archive before publication.
The hero and social crops are FMB-owned editorial graphics using the approved FMB icon and are explicitly not documentary photographs.
